PLATE NO. 12 • MATIA MAHAL, JAMA MASJID

The Nihari Master of Jama Masjid

In the labyrinth of Matia Mahal, Haji Shabrati’s descendants still wake at midnight to tend the copper degs that have slow-cooked Shahjahanabad’s defining stew for generations.

WRITTEN BY Siddharth Shah
14 MINUTE READ

To enter Matia Mahal as the morning mist begins to lift is to witness a theater of scent and steam. While the rest of Delhi sleeps under a canopy of smog, the lane facing the grand sandstone arches of the Jama Masjid is wide awake, breathing in the rich, heavy perfume of slow-rendered bone marrow, crushed cloves, and toasted flour.

At the epicenter of this ritual sits Haji Shabrati Nihari Wale. Established in 1957, but carrying forward a technical lineage that predates the Mutiny of 1857, this modest shop front is a temple of subtraction. There are no menus, no expansive spreads of side dishes. There is only the degh, a massive, bell-shaped copper vessel sealed with dough, and the legacy of Haji Shabrati himself.

"The heat must crawl through the heavy copper. If you rush Nihari, you are not cooking; you are simply boiling meat. The bone must give up its marrow to the gravy, or it is not Shabrati's."

The technique is rigorous. The buffalo meat is layered carefully with spices, ghee, and water before the pot is sealed. A slow fire of charcoal embers is stoked beneath. For eight to ten hours, the stew undergoes a slow transformation. The tough cuts of meat soften until they can be parted with the light pressure of a thumb, and the fat rises to the surface as an amber oil known as tari.

Haji Shabrati presiding over the morning's first service, Matia Mahal. CREDIT: DEVESH SHARMA

When the seal is broken at dawn, a line of loyalists has already gathered on the damp cobblestones outside. The server, armed with a long-handled copper ladle, portioning the meat with practiced grace. First, a piece of exceptionally tender meat is laid in a shallow ceramic bowl; next, a ladle of the thick, spiced broth; and finally, a precise splash of the fiery red oil gathered from the top of the pot.

The dish is served piping hot, adorned only with a pinch of fresh ginger juliennes, chopped green chilies, and a squeeze of lime. It is eaten with warm, leavened Khamiri Roti, fresh from the clay tandoor down the lane.

ANATOMY OF A LEGACY

The Shahjahanabad Spice Profile

Unlike modern commercial approximations, a true Old Delhi Nihari relies heavily on warming spices (garam masalas) that target the chest and respiratory system during the damp, cold winters of the north.

Peepal (Long Pepper) Provides an initial sharp heat that lingers at the back of the palate, distinct from green chilies.
Javitri & Jaiphal Mace and nutmeg, freshly grated, introducing an essential sweet, woodsy fragrance.
Khas (Vetiver Roots) Often enclosed in a muslin pouch during stewing to impart a subtle, cooling earthy depth.
Sauf (Fennel Seeds) Toasted and ground incredibly fine to act as both a cooling aromatic and a natural digestive.
CURRENT COST PER SERVING ₹180

Haji Shabrati (c. 1957)
LOCATION
Shop 722, Haveli Azam Khan, Chitli Qabar, Matiya Mahal, Delhi-6

FROM THE ARCHIVE

"The Mughal army's doctors designed Nihari to combat the harsh Delhi winter. It was meant to be eaten at dawn, followed by a long sleep before the day's duties."

— Dr. S. Alvi, Delhi College (1912)
